verses.15:9: And Pilate answered them, saying, "Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?"
verses.15:10: For he knew that it was because of envy that the chief priests had handed Him over.
verses.15:11: But the chief priests stirred up the crowd so that he would instead release Barabbas for them.
verses.15:12: And answering again, Pilate said to them, "Then what should I do with the One you call the King of the Jews?"
verses.15:13: And they cried out again, "Crucify Him!"
verses.15:14: But Pilate said to them, "Why, what evil has He done?" Yet they cried out all the more, "Crucify Him!"
verses.15:15: So Pilate, wanting to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas for them, and after having Jesus flogged, he handed Him over so that He might be crucified.
verses.15:16: Then the soldiers led Him away inside the courtyard, which is the Praetorium, and they called together the entire cohort.
verses.15:17: And they dressed Him in purple, and after weaving a crown of thorns, they placed it on Him.
verses.15:18: And they began to salute Him, "Hail, King of the Jews!"
verses.15:19: And they kept striking His head with a reed and spitting on Him, and bending their knees, they were bowing in homage to Him.
verses.15:20: And when they had mocked Him, they stripped the purple off Him and put His own garments on Him. And they led Him out to crucify Him.
verses.15:21: And they pressed into service a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the countryside, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry His cross.
verses.15:22: And they brought Him to the place Golgotha, which is translated, "Place of a Skull."
verses.15:23: And they tried to give Him wine mixed with myrrh, but He did not take it.
verses.15:24: And they crucified Him and divided His garments among themselves, casting lots for them as to who should take what.
verses.15:25: Now it was the third hour, and they crucified Him.
verses.15:26: And the inscription of the charge against Him had been written: "The King of the Jews."
verses.15:27: And with Him they crucified two robbers, one on His right and one on His left.
verses.15:29: And those passing by kept reviling Him, shaking their heads and saying, "Aha! You who destroy the temple and build it in three days,
verses.15:30: save Yourself by coming down from the cross!"
verses.15:31: In the same way, the chief priests also, mocking Him among themselves together with the scribes, were saying, "He saved others; He cannot save Himself.
verses.15:32: Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe!" And those who were crucified with Him were reproaching Him.
verses.15:33: And when the sixth hour came, darkness fell over the whole land until the ninth hour.
verses.15:34: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?" which is translated, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?"
verses.15:35: And some of those standing nearby, hearing this, were saying, "Look, He is calling Elijah."
verses.15:36: Then someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed, and offered it to Him to drink, saying, "Wait, let us see if Elijah is coming to take Him down."
verses.15:37: And Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed His last.
verses.15:38: And the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.
verses.15:39: Now when the centurion, who was standing directly opposite Him, saw that He breathed His last in this way, he said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!"
verses.15:40: There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were both Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome,
verses.15:41: who, when He was in Galilee, used to follow Him and serve Him, as well as many other women who had come up with Him to Jerusalem.
verses.15:42: And when evening had already arrived, since it was Preparation Day, that is, the day before the Sabbath,
verses.15:43: Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council who himself was also waiting for the kingdom of God, came, and gathering his courage, went in to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
verses.15:44: And Pilate was surprised that He was already dead, and summoning the centurion, he questioned him as to whether He had died some time ago.
verses.15:45: And when he learned this from the centurion, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
verses.15:46: And after buying a linen cloth, he took Him down, wrapped Him in the linen cloth, and laid Him in a tomb that had been cut out of rock; and he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb.
verses.15:47: Now Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses were watching where He had been laid.
verses.16:1: And when the Sabbath had passed, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they might come and anoint Him.
verses.16:2: And very early on the first day of the week, once the sun had risen, they came to the tomb.
verses.16:3: And they were saying among themselves, "Who will roll the stone away for us from the doorway of the tomb?"
verses.16:4: And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away, for it was extremely large.
verses.16:5: And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, wearing a white robe, and they were alarmed.
verses.16:6: And he said to them, "Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has been raised; He is not here. Look at the place where they laid Him.
verses.16:7: But go, tell His disciples and Peter that He is going ahead of you into Galilee; there you will see Him, just as He told you."
verses.16:8: And going out, they fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
verses.16:9: ⟦Now after He had risen early on the first day of the week, He appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom He had cast out seven demons.⟧
verses.16:10: ⟦She went and reported it to those who had been with Him, while they were mourning and weeping.⟧
verses.16:11: ⟦And when they heard that He was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe.⟧
verses.16:12: ⟦After these things, He appeared in another form to two of them as they were walking along, going into the countryside.⟧
verses.16:13: ⟦And they went away and reported it to the rest, yet they did not believe them either.⟧
verses.16:14: ⟦Afterward, He appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and He reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen Him after He was raised.⟧
verses.16:15: ⟦And He said to them, "Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation.⟧

notes.1:1: The title "Son of God" is included in the Saints Greek Critical Text and most manuscripts (such as B, D, and W), though it is omitted in a few early witnesses, including the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus.
notes.1:2: Mark introduces a composite quotation blending Exodus 23:20, Malachi 3:1, and Isaiah 40:3 under the name of Isaiah, the major prophet whose passage forms the climax in verse 3.
notes.1:27: The phrase "with authority" may either qualify "a new teaching" or introduce "He commands even the unclean spirits"; this translation follows the punctuation of the Greek text, connecting it with the verb "commands."
notes.1:41: While nearly all Greek manuscripts read "moved with compassion" (splanchnistheis), Codex Bezae (D) and several Old Latin witnesses read "moved with anger" (orgistheis).
notes.1:43: Both verbs here are notably forceful: "sternly warning" (embrimesamenos) conveys urgent intensity, and "sent him away" (exebalen) is the same Greek verb used of driving out demons in verses 34 and 39.
notes.2:10: The mid-sentence shift from addressing the scribes to addressing the paralyzed man reflects an abrupt grammatical break (anacoluthon) present in the Greek text.
notes.2:19: "Sons of the bridal chamber" is a Semitic idiom referring to the bridegroom's attendants or wedding guests.
notes.2:23: "Make their way" renders the Greek expression hodon poiein (literally "make a path"), meaning either to travel along or to clear a path while plucking heads of grain.
notes.2:26: "In the time of Abiathar the high priest" is a noted historical crux because 1 Samuel 21:1-6 names Abiathar's father, Ahimelech, as the priest at Nob; the phrase may point broadly to the era or narrative cycle associated with Abiathar, who became David's prominent high priest.
notes.3:14: Some manuscripts omit "whom He also named apostles" here (and "and He appointed the twelve" in 3:16), likely to smooth the repetition; both clauses stand in the critical text.
notes.3:18: "Cananaean" transliterates an Aramaic term meaning "zealous one" or "Zealot" (compare Luke 6:15) rather than indicating an inhabitant of Canaan.
notes.3:21: "His own people" (literally "those beside Him") is an idiom for Jesus' family or relatives (compare 3:31), while "they were saying" is an indefinite plural that may refer either to His family or to people in general.
notes.3:29: "An eternal sin" (Greek aioniou hamartematos) is supported by the earliest manuscripts; later manuscripts substitute "eternal judgment" (kriseos).
notes.4:8: Greek εἰς τριάκοντα καὶ ἓν ἑξήκοντα καὶ ἓν ἑκατόν (literally "to thirty and one-sixty and one-hundred") reflects a Semitic multiplicative idiom meaning thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold; the same ἓν idiom recurs in 4:20.
notes.4:12: The conjunction ἵνα ("so that") can express either purpose or result, echoing Isaiah 6:9-10; the paired participles and finite verbs ("seeing they may see", "hearing they may hear") preserve a Hebraic emphatic idiom.
notes.4:29: Greek παραδοῖ literally means "yields itself" or "permits," an intransitive agricultural idiom for a crop becoming ripe, while "sends forth the sickle" echoes Joel 3:13 (LXX 4:13).
notes.4:39: The command πεφίμωσο ("Be still!") is a perfect passive imperative literally meaning "Be muzzled!" or "Stay silenced!", the same verb used to silence an unclean spirit in Mark 1:25.
notes.5:1: Early manuscripts vary between "Gerasenes" (the reading translated here), "Gadarenes," and "Gergesenes," reflecting ancient efforts to align the name with the geography of the Sea of Galilee.
notes.5:23: The Greek verb translated "be made well" (also in 5:28 and 5:34) is the standard term for "save," encompassing both physical healing and spiritual deliverance.
notes.5:36: The Greek participle translated "disregarding" (parakousas) can mean either "ignoring/paying no attention to" or "overhearing."
notes.5:41: "Talitha koum" is a transliteration of the Aramaic command "Little girl, rise"; some later manuscripts spell the second word "koumi."
notes.6:3: Greek tekton denotes a skilled craftsman or builder working in wood, stone, or metal, traditionally rendered "carpenter."
notes.6:9: The Greek shifts abruptly from indirect discourse (v. 8) to a second-person direct command ("do not put on two tunics"), smoothed here into English.
notes.6:20: Following the earliest manuscripts (eporei, "was greatly perplexed"); other manuscripts read epoiei ("did many things").
notes.6:22: Following the oldest manuscripts reading "his daughter Herodias" (autou Herodiados); other manuscripts smooth the text to "Herodias's own daughter" (autes tes Herodiados). Josephus names Herodias's daughter Salome.
notes.6:40: Greek prasiai prasiai literally means "garden-beds, garden-beds," picturing the crowd seated in neat rectangular plots on the green grass.
notes.7:3: Greek pygme literally means 'with the fist,' a debated idiom variously understood as washing with a cupped hand, up to the wrist, or thoroughly; some manuscripts read pykna ('often').
notes.7:15: Verse 16 ('If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear') is absent from the earliest manuscripts; this critical text prints it in double brackets ⟦ ⟧.
notes.7:19: The masculine participle katharizon ('declaring clean,' literally 'cleansing') refers back to Jesus ('He said' in v. 18), marking Mark's editorial comment on the implication of the saying.
notes.7:22: 'An evil eye' (ophthalmos poneros) is a literal idiom denoting envy, stinginess, or grudging malice.
notes.8:12: Literally "if a sign will be given to this generation," a Semitic elliptical oath idiom expressing an emphatic negation.
notes.8:20: Mark distinguishes two kinds of baskets in 8:19 and 8:20: kophinos (v. 19) is a smaller hand-basket, whereas spyris (vv. 8, 20) is a large woven hamper.
notes.8:26: Some later manuscripts expand Jesus' command with "nor tell anyone in the village," whereas the earliest witnesses preserve the shorter text translated here.
notes.8:35: The Greek word psyche (also in vv. 36-37) spans both physical "life" and one's inner "soul" or "self."
notes.9:16: The Greek text reads the reflexive pronoun 'αὑτούς' ('among yourselves' / 'with one another'); other editions read 'αὐτούς' ('with them', referring to the disciples).
notes.9:23: The Greek places the definite article 'Τό' before 'Εἰ δύνῃ' ('The "If You can"!'), quoting and challenging the father's hesitant condition from verse 22.
notes.9:29: Several early manuscripts (including Codex Vaticanus) end the verse with 'by prayer'; most others add 'and fasting'.
notes.9:43: 'Gehenna' transliterates the Greek name for the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, used for the place of final fiery judgment. Verses 44 and 46, which repeat verse 48 in later manuscripts, are absent from the earliest witnesses.
notes.9:49: Later manuscripts add 'and every sacrifice will be salted with salt' (compare Leviticus 2:13).
notes.10:7: Some later manuscripts add 'and be joined to his wife' (cf. Gen 2:24; Matt 19:5), which is absent from the earliest manuscripts followed in this text.
notes.10:24: Some manuscripts expand this saying to read 'for those who trust in wealth to enter the kingdom of God,' whereas the earliest witnesses attest the shorter text translated here.
notes.10:26: The Greek text reads 'to Him' (pros auton) rather than 'to one another' (pros heautous), which appears in some other manuscripts.
notes.10:45: The preposition anti basically means 'in place of' or 'in exchange for'; lytron denotes a price paid to release captives or slaves.
notes.10:52: The verb sozo ('save') is also used of physical healing ('make well').
notes.11:3: The closing clause ("and immediately He will send it back here") can be punctuated either as part of the disciples' promise that the Lord will promptly return the colt, or as Jesus' assurance that the owner will immediately send it to Him.
notes.11:22: Literally "Have faith of God"; the genitive is usually taken objectively as "faith in God," though some read it as "faith from God" or "God's faithfulness."
notes.11:24: The verb elabete is aorist, literally 'you received.'
notes.11:25: The verse numbered 11:26 in later manuscripts (a parallel to Matthew 6:15) is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts; this text prints it in double brackets.
notes.11:32: The leaders' question breaks off mid-thought (aposiopesis) as the narrator interjects the reason for their hesitation.
notes.12:4: The rare Greek verb ekephaliosan occurs only here in the New Testament and literally denotes striking or wounding someone on the head.
notes.12:26: "At the bush" is an idiomatic reference to the section of the book of Exodus concerning the burning bush (Exodus 3), used before chapter and verse divisions existed.
notes.12:36: The critical text reads hypokato ("beneath"), whereas some manuscripts assimilate to the Septuagint of Psalm 110:1 by reading hypopodion ("a footstool").
notes.12:42: A lepton was the smallest Jewish copper coin in circulation; two lepta equaled one Roman quadrans, worth approximately 1/64 of a denarius (a day's wage).
notes.13:6: The Greek phrase "I am" (ego eimi) has no expressed predicate; it may mean "I am he" (the Christ) or echo the divine self-designation.
notes.13:14: The Greek participle for "standing" (hestekota) is masculine even though "abomination" (bdelygma) is neuter, pointing to a personal figure or image.
notes.13:29: Greek expresses no subject for "is near"; it may refer either to "it" (the fulfillment of these events) or to "He" (the Son of Man).
notes.13:33: The words "and pray" (kai proseuchesthe) appear in this Greek text (following many manuscripts), though they are absent from several early Alexandrian witnesses.
notes.14:3: The Greek adjective pistikes describing nard is uncertain in meaning; it is most commonly taken as "genuine" or "pure," though some interpret it as "liquid" or as a loanword denoting a specific variety of nard.
notes.14:10: The Greek verb paradidomi literally means "hand over" or "deliver up" and is used consistently across verses 10, 11, 18, and 21, carrying the sense of betrayal in Judas's action.
notes.14:24: The critical Greek text reads "My blood of the covenant" without the word "new," which was added in later manuscripts in assimilation to Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25.
notes.14:36: "Abba" is the Aramaic word for "Father," which Mark retains and immediately translates into Greek as ho pater.
notes.14:41: The Greek verb apechei ("It is enough") is unusual here and is sometimes understood in a commercial sense ("It is settled" or "The account is paid"); the preceding verbs ("sleeping and taking your rest") can be read either as a question or as an ironic imperative.
notes.14:62: "The Power" (tes dynameos) is a reverential Jewish circumlocution for God, matching "the Blessed One" in verse 61.
notes.14:68: The critical Greek text ends this verse at "forecourt"; many later manuscripts add "and a rooster crowed" to align with Jesus's prediction in verse 30 and the second crowing in verse 72.
notes.14:72: The Greek participle epibalon is famously difficult and debated; interpreters have variously understood it as "breaking down," "thinking about it," "covering his head," or "rushing out."
notes.15:25: "The third hour" corresponds to roughly 9:00 a.m. in ancient daylight reckoning; likewise, the sixth and ninth hours in 15:33-34 correspond to about noon and 3:00 p.m.
notes.15:27: The earliest Greek manuscripts lack verse 28 (printed in double brackets in this text), which probably entered later manuscripts from Luke 22:37.
notes.15:34: Jesus quotes Psalm 22:1 in Aramaic ("Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?"), whose opening sounds resemble the name Elijah, explaining the bystanders' misunderstanding in verse 35.
notes.15:39: The predicate huios theou has no article and stands before the verb, so it can be translated either 'the Son of God' or 'a son of God.'
notes.16:8: The earliest and most reliable manuscripts (including Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus) end the Gospel of Mark here at verse 8, leaving open whether this abrupt ending was intentional or whether an original ending was lost.
notes.16:9: Verses 9-20 (marked with double brackets) comprise the traditional "Longer Ending" of Mark; this section is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts and exhibits vocabulary and style distinct from the rest of the Gospel.
notes.16:18: Some manuscripts include minor variants in this passage (such as adding "in their hands" with "pick up serpents"), reflecting early textual variation within the Longer Ending.
